title: Emergency Evacuation
summary: A disorganized evacuation can cause confusion, injury, and property damage. Everyone should know the alarm, the routes, the assembly area, and who is in charge before an emergency happens.
talking_points: Know how to report a fire or other emergency and what the alarm sounds like. Alarms must be distinctive and recognized by all as a signal to evacuate.
Know the primary and secondary evacuation routes and exits for your work area.
Routes and exits should be clearly marked, well lit, wide enough for everyone, and clear of debris at all times.
Know who is in charge of emergencies. That person has the authority to order an evacuation or shutdown.
Go to the assembly area after you leave. A head count is taken so no one is missed.
Do not go back in to look for someone. Report their name and last known location to the person in charge.
Leave rescue work to people who are trained, equipped, and certified. Untrained rescuers can endanger themselves and others.
Look out for coworkers who may need extra help, use the buddy system, and avoid hazardous areas during an evacuation.
site_hazards_to_check: Evacuation routes or exits blocked or cluttered with debris
Routes not marked or poorly lit
No posted evacuation procedures or route drawings
No designated assembly area or head-count method
Alarm that not everyone can hear, see, or recognize
No plan for helping people with disabilities or who do not speak English
discussion_questions: What is our alarm signal, and where is our assembly area?
Who has the authority to order an evacuation on this site?
Why should untrained people not attempt a rescue?
